references.title: Army Regulation 25-50: Preparing and Managing Correspondence
references.note: Army writing standard: bottom line up front, active voice, ~15-word average sentences, avoid opening with It is / There is / There are.

references.title: Speechwriting in Perspective: A Brief Guide to Effective and Persuasive Communication (98-170)
references.note: Spoken sentences average 8-16 words; ~2,600 words per 20 minutes; speakers range 115-175 wpm.

references.title: How to write jokes that aren't funny
references.note: Jokes undercut emotion; stop joking when things turn serious, or use jokes that keep the pain visible.

references.title: Single-Camera vs. Multi-Camera TV Sitcom Scripts: What's the Difference
references.note: Single-cam 22-32 pages, multi-cam 52-58 pages for ~22 minutes; multi-cam double-spaces dialogue.

references.title: Does one page of a screenplay really equal one minute of screen time?
references.note: Mean ~55 s per page; only 18.2% of scripts within ±5%; suggested rule 1 page ~ 1 minute ±20%.

references.title: Fountain 1.1 Syntax
references.note: Notes sit between [[ and ]]; a truly empty line ends a note; sections and synopses do not print.

references.title: If any subtitles/captions are used, present them in a clear, easy to read way
references.note: At most 40 characters per line and 2 lines per subtitle.

references.title: Voice and tone (Google developer documentation style guide)
references.note: Avoid please, simply, it's easy, quickly and placeholder phrases such as at this time in instructions.

references.title: Sentence length: why 25 words is our limit
references.note: Break up or condense sentences over 25 words; supporting comprehension figures are second-hand.

references.title: Writing with ink
references.note: Loose ends are errors (ran out of content); choice sets need fallbacks.

references.title: Readability formulas, programs and tools: Do they work for plain language?
references.note: Rewriting to lower a formula score does not raise comprehension.

references.authors: Mac, Ayre, McCaffery, Boroumand, Bell, Muscat
references.title: The Readability Study: A Randomised Trial of Health Information Written at Different Grade Reading Levels
references.note: No comprehension difference between grade 8 and grade 14 versions.

references.title: The passive voice and comprehensibility of biomedical texts: an experimental study with 2 cohorts of chiropractic students
references.note: Active rewrites changed neither length, readability nor comprehension.

references.title: Plain Language Is for Everyone, Even Experts
references.note: Experts also prefer plain text; no more than 15-20 words per sentence.

references.title: Does Writing with Language Models Reduce Content Diversity?
references.note: Writing with an instruction-tuned model lowered lexical diversity and repeated model-supplied phrases.

references.authors: Association for Psychological Science (report of a Steven Pinker address)
references.title: The Curse of Knowledge: Pinker Describes a Key Cause of Bad Writing
references.note: Classic style avoids hedges such as somewhat, nearly, relatively and apparently.

references.title: Beyond Branching: Quality-Based, Salience-Based, and Waypoint Narrative Structures
references.note: Salience systems need broad fallbacks; used content is down-weighted for variety.

references.authors: Writers Guild of America West (Nastaran Dibai)
references.title: Ask a Mentor: Switching from Drama to Comedy Rooms
references.note: Scenes are funnier when the scene has a comic premise; jokes grow out of it.

references.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
references.note: Science Advances 11(27). Abstract-only in our notes: style words such as delves, showcasing and underscores rose abruptly in PubMed abstracts after 2022; the paper dates the vocabulary, which is why entries carry eras.

references.title: Why Does ChatGPT "Delve" So Much? Exploring the Sources of Lexical Overrepresentation in Large Language Models
references.note: COLING 2025. Abstract-only in our notes: 21 focal words overrepresented in scientific abstracts; no evidence the cause is architecture or training data; consistent with a role for human-feedback tuning.

references.authors: Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu and Zou
references.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
references.note: Patterns 4(7). Abstract-only in our notes: seven detectors misjudged non-native English essays as machine-written (61.3% average false-positive rate on 91 TOEFL essays) while classifying native essays accurately.

references.authors: Liang, Zhang, Wu, Izzo, Ouyang and others
references.title: Mapping the Increasing Use of LLMs in Scientific Papers
references.note: COLM 2024. Abstract-only in our notes: a population-level estimate of LLM-modified text across 950,965 papers from 2020 to February 2024; says nothing about any single document.

references.authors: Reinhart, Markey, Laudenbach, Pantusen, Yurko, Weinberg and Brown
references.title: Do LLMs write like humans? Variation in grammatical and rhetorical styles
references.note: PNAS 122(8). Abstract-only in our notes: with Biber's lexical, grammatical and rhetorical features, instruction-tuned models differ systematically from human writing and from each other.

references.title: People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text
references.note: ACL 2025. Abstract-only in our notes: frequent users of the tools judged 300 articles far better than most automatic detectors, relying on lexical clues and on formality, originality and clarity; that judgement is not codifiable here.

references.title: The Last Fingerprint: How Markdown Training Shapes LLM Prose
references.note: arXiv preprint; peer-review status was not confirmed. Abstract-only in our notes: across twelve models from five providers, em dash rates ran from 0.0 to 9.1 per 1,000 words, so the rate depends on the model.

references.title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing
references.note: Era-tagged vocabulary, copula avoidance, chatbot artifacts; descriptive signs, not proof of authorship.

references.title: How suitable are TED talks for academic listening?
references.note: TED talks are significantly faster than lectures.

references.title: BBC Subtitle Guidelines
references.note: Subtitle timing assumes speech at 160-180 words per minute.

references.title: Xbox Accessibility Guideline 104: Subtitles and captions
references.note: Avoid lines over 40 characters; at most 2 lines on screen; label speakers.

references.title: Saliency
references.note: Line groups pick the most specific match and prefer least-recently-viewed lines.

references.title: Strengthening enforcement against egregious clickbait on YouTube
references.note: Titles and thumbnails must not promise what the video does not deliver.

references.title: Measure key moments for audience retention
references.note: The intro metric is retention at 30 seconds, read as whether the opening matched the title and thumbnail.

references.title: Formatting Your Spec Script, a Primer: Part 20
references.note: Multi-cam: description in ALL CAPS, dialogue double-spaced, lettered scenes, character list under headings.

references.title: Analysis: Conversation Design in Games
references.note: Hub-and-spoke repetition makes an implausibly patient NPC; repeat visits need variants or summaries.

references.title: Procedures (Google developer documentation style guide)
references.note: One action per step; first sentence of a step includes an imperative verb; a single-step procedure is a bullet.

references.title: Writing step-by-step instructions (Microsoft Writing Style Guide)
references.note: Start each step with an imperative verb unless a short location phrase comes first.

references.title: Minimalism Reconsidered
references.note: Cutting information causes task failure; procedures need explicit steps and recovery.

references.title: From stage to page: language independent bootstrap measures of distinctiveness in fictional speech
references.note: Character voice distinctiveness is measurable; canonical playwrights' characters separate.

references.title: Best Practices for Game Localization (v22)
references.note: Character style guides should be concrete: period, region, register and real samples.

references.title: Sonnet (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Reference glossary entry, not a study: traditionally 14 lines of iambic pentameter; Petrarchan abbaabba then cdecde or cdcdcd with a turn after line 8; Shakespearean abab cdcd efef gg. The entry says "traditionally" and "one of several rhyme schemes".

references.title: Villanelle (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Reference glossary entry, not a study: 19 lines, five tercets and a quatrain, A1 b A2 / a b A1 / a b A2 / a b A1 / a b A2 / a b A1 A2. Notes that contemporary poets have loosened the refrains. Gives no meter.

references.title: Sestina (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Reference glossary entry, not a study: 39 lines, six six-line stanzas rotating six end words (ABCDEF, FAEBDC, CFDABE, ECBFAD, DEACFB, BDFECA) and a three-line envoi holding all six. Lines may be any length; no rhyme scheme.

references.title: Limerick (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Reference glossary entry, not a study: five lines, AABBA (the fifth line repeats the first or rhymes with it), anapestic, three stresses on lines 1, 2 and 5 and two on lines 3 and 4.

references.title: Haiku (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Reference glossary entry, not a study: a traditional Japanese haiku is three lines in 5/7/5, and the entry says the form's regular traits, including the syllable pattern, have been routinely broken.

references.title: Ballad (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Reference glossary entry, not a study: quatrain stanzas, lines with as few as three or four stresses, rhymed on the second and fourth lines or on all alternating lines.

references.title: Enjambment (Glossary of Poetic Terms)
references.note: Reference glossary entry, not a study: defines enjambment against the end-stopped line and says without punctuation lines run on faster. Gives no way to detect it mechanically.

references.authors: Obermeier, Menninghaus, von Koppenfels, Raettig, Schmidt-Kassow, Otterbein and Kotz
references.title: Aesthetic and emotional effects of meter and rhyme in poetry
references.note: 17 native German speakers rated recorded four-line stanzas; metered and rhymed versions were liked more. Small sample, German poetry heard aloud, end rhyme present or absent only.

references.title: EEG correlates of song prosody: a new look at the relationship between linguistic and musical rhythm
references.note: 16 analysed participants heard sung six-syllable sentences; stress aligned with the beat eased word recognition. Lab sentences on tonal sequences, not real songs or lyrics.

references.title: AI-generated poetry is indistinguishable from human-written poetry and is rated more favorably
references.note: Scientific Reports, two pre-registered studies on non-expert readers; ChatGPT 3.5 poems against poems by 10 canonical poets. The paper itself, not a news summary.

references.title: PhonologyBench: Evaluating Phonological Skills of Large Language Models
references.note: arXiv preprint (v1); peer-review status was not confirmed. Six 2024-era LLMs on grapheme-to-phoneme, syllable counting and rhyme generation, American English; gold syllable counts come from a G2P library.

references.title: Sonnet or Not, Bot? Poetry Evaluation for Large Models and Datasets
references.note: arXiv preprint (v3); peer-review status was not confirmed. A form-recognition benchmark of over 4.1k annotated poems; says poetic forms are "likely to be stretched or broken by poets".

references.title: Prosodic: a metrical-phonological parser for English and Finnish
references.note: The project's own documentation and self-reported figures: rhyme classed as perfect, slant (consonance), assonance or none from the sounds after the last stressed vowel; bands fitted to Walker's 1775 rhyming dictionary.

references.title: CMU US English pronouncing dictionary
references.note: US English only. The maintainers do not guarantee accuracy and "expect a number of errors, omissions and inconsistencies to remain"; the flat file carries no part of speech and handles reduced variants inconsistently.

references.title: Songwriting Tools and Techniques (course page)
references.note: Weak evidence: a course description and syllabus. It lists topics (matching musical stress and syllable stress, line length, common meter, rhyme types) without defining them or giving thresholds.

references.title: Songwriting: Writing the Lyrics (course page)
references.note: Weak evidence: a marketing and course-description page. It says learners judge whether a lyric is stable or unstable through line lengths, number of lines, stress and melody, with no definition or threshold.

references.title: Anatomy of a Song: The Three Most Common Song Forms
references.note: Weak evidence: a practitioner teaching article. Describes verse-chorus, refrain and AABA forms; its 95% figure is unsourced and not used; the author says none of it "is a rule or a formula".

references.title: Scansion
references.note: Weak evidence: an encyclopedia summary (no allowed kind fits an encyclopedia article, so the nearest is practitioner, as for wikipedia-signs-ai). Its claims rest on citations that were not checked here.

references.title: CommonMark Spec
references.note: The Markdown specification the parser follows: a line starting with a list marker, a number and a period, > or # starts a list item, ordered list, block quote or heading.
